selvedge: A woven collection for rooms that change with the light.

A curtain, a cushion and a bench cover catch the same afternoon light differently. This collection starts with that observation. The lightest weave lets the window frame show through. The middle weight takes a clean fold. The heaviest gives the bench a continuous line.
The collection shares a narrow palette so a designer can put all three weights in one room. Each sample is large enough to hang, gather and view from across a table.
Seen from across the room, the curtain reads as a pale field. Up close, the gaps between yarns let the wall colour enter the cloth. That small shift is most apparent where two folds cross.
In the sample room we hang one width flat beside a gathered length. The pair shows a client how much the appearance changes once the cloth takes on volume.
A pale ground for the sheer. Hang it against the actual wall before selecting a lining.
A muted olive for the middle weight. Its darker cross thread brings out the ridge of each fold.
A warm red used on binding and small upholstered pieces. A narrow edge is enough to carry it across a room.

Each trial starts with a short length of warp and a numbered weft. The weaver saves a cutting before finishing and a second cutting afterwards. Both stay on the same sheet, so the difference in handle can be discussed alongside the change in colour.
For the next trial we change one thread or one finishing step. That makes the sample book a record of decisions a second weaver can follow.

Three trial cloths use the same family of colours. The example weights are 120, 240 and 420 grams per square metre. The gap between them matters when a length hangs from a narrow rail or wraps a curved corner.
These sample specifications guide the first mock-up. The studio confirms the finished lot and tests it for the intended application before a production order.
Turn the visible face around the edge so the front reads as one continuous surface.
A narrow madder binding catches the seam and gives the upholsterer a visible reference line.
Keep a separate cutting of the backing with the prototype so later repairs can match the assembly.
A flat swatch hides the way a curtain breaks where it meets the floor. For this trial two equal lengths share one rail. One is gathered tightly and one loosely, with the window behind both.
The buyer can move the cloth and see the difference in shadow. Notes on the back of the sample card record the spacing used in the room.
Cut one flat reference and one handling swatch from each finished trial. Mark the warp direction on the reverse.
Hang the sheer and fit the heavy cloth to one bench corner. Photograph both in morning and afternoon light.
Keep the chosen pieces with the order sheet. Send the workroom a matched set before cutting the first roll.

The archive keeps a handling piece at the front and a protected reference behind it. Each card carries the trial number, finish and date. A client can take the handling piece to site while the studio retains a comparison for the next delivery.
Return notes matter most when they name a condition: direct window light, a curved seat or a seam under tension. Those details make the next consultation more precise.
Confirm the window, furniture and light conditions with a simple survey and a photograph taken from the entrance.
Approve a hung length and a finished corner with the people who will make the final pieces.
File the approved swatches, confirmed quantities and workroom notes under a single commission number.
Take the cloth into the room
Choose one weight to hang, one to fold and one to wrap. Compare them under the light the finished pieces will live in.
gatefold-cinema: One platform. Two night workers. Eleven minutes before the first departure.

A station cleaner discovers a small cassette player under a bench. Its handwritten label carries the name of the signal operator upstairs. Bringing it back means leaving the platform halfway through the last cleaning round of the night.

The film follows that short walk in real time. As the first passengers arrive downstairs, an ordinary handover becomes the last private conversation the two workers will have before the shift changes.

The opening frame looks down the platform from bench height. The cleaner enters at its far end and crosses the length of the shot before the cassette comes into view. The audience learns the scale of the walk by watching it happen.
Keep the station name outside the frame. Paint, tile and the spacing of the lights give the location its identity.
Hold the length of the platform as a worker moves through it. Footsteps announce the character before a face is visible.
At the stairwell, move close enough to read the hand around the player. The operator remains behind glass.
Save the first close view for the play button. A thumb hovering over it gives the audience a beat to listen.

The tape carries a rehearsal recorded years earlier. We hear its first notes through the player's small speaker. The sound stays narrow and local while the station ventilation continues underneath it.
Let a train announcement briefly cover the melody. When the voice ends, the two workers are still listening and the audience hears the room again.

The proposed cut spends four minutes on the platform, two in the stairwell, three in the booth and two back at the gate. The longest uninterrupted passage belongs to the approach, when the cleaner has time to change their mind.
The edit can borrow seconds between passages. Keep enough silence after the cassette starts for both people to react before cutting away.
Stops one step below the door and holds out the player. The hand stays inside the frame throughout the exchange.
Opens the door partway, recognises the label and steps back. The invitation is visible before either person speaks.
Waits on the landing until the operator moves. Crossing the threshold becomes a decision the audience can share.

The booth has its own pool of light. Through the glass the platform is still visible, now with a handful of waiting passengers. Keep that second space readable so the approaching departure remains present during the conversation.
A reflection can briefly place the cleaner beside the operator before both appear in the same physical frame.
Rehearse the walk and handover in a marked space. Record the time it takes to reach the door at the actor's natural pace.
Capture the wide platform passage first. Move to the landing while the practical lights and ambient sound remain consistent.
Record room tone in each space, plus the player opening, the door closing and the train leaving the platform.

The cleaner returns downstairs while the operator rewinds the tape. The first passengers pass between the camera and the bench, briefly hiding the spot where the player was found. Hold until the platform clears again.
End on the next ordinary task: the cleaner turns the bucket toward the exit. The audience has seen enough of the earlier route to recognise the change in pace.
Check that the cleaner's hand remains legible against the dark coat and that reflections leave both faces visible.
Test the cassette on a small speaker as well as the screening system. The first note should be recognisable in both rooms.
Leave a short bed of station ambience under the first credit, then let the room fall quiet.
As the train pulls away, the music continues upstairs. The last thing we see is the empty bench in the first light of day.
